title: Exterior glaze pouring technique
subtitle: Pouring glaze over the outside of a bisqueware vessel for even coverage
excerpt: Pouring glaze over the exterior of a bisqueware vessel is faster than brushing and produces a more even coat. The vessel is held upside-down over a catch bucket and glaze is poured from a jug in a smooth spiralling motion. The foot ring is then cleaned of glaze before firing. Suitable for bowls, vases, and tall cylinders.
sourceNotes: Glaze pouring technique derived from standard pottery practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Clay that has been fired once to harden it but has not yet been glazed; it is porous and holds wet glaze well
The raised ring at the base of a wheel-thrown piece; must be cleaned of glaze before firing to prevent the piece sticking to the kiln shelf

content.text: Glaze materials contain silica and may contain metallic oxide colourants including iron, cobalt, copper, manganese, and barium. Wear a dust mask rated FFP2 or N95 when measuring and mixing dry glaze materials. Do not eat or drink in the glazing area. Keep glaze away from children. Fire in a kiln with good ventilation; do not remain in the kiln room during firing.
Pouring is the most efficient way to glaze the exterior of a
piece when you need a uniform single-coat coverage. It requires a catch bucket to reclaim the poured glaze and a wax-resist or sponge pass on the
after pouring to prevent the piece sticking to the kiln shelf during firing.

materials.name: Mixed glaze at pouring consistency (similar to semi-skimmed milk)
Wax resist (optional, to protect foot ring)

content.text: If the interior is to be glazed, do that first by pouring glaze inside and rotating to coat, then draining. Allow the interior glaze to dry fully before proceeding to the exterior pour.
Apply wax resist to the foot ring with the liner brush. Allow to dry for 15 minutes. Alternatively, clean the foot ring with a damp sponge after pouring.
Stir the glaze thoroughly before pouring. Check the consistency: dip your hand in and observe the film on skin. It should coat like a smooth cream and not run off immediately.

Hold the vessel upside-down over the catch bucket by the foot ring between two fingers. Pour the glaze from a jug in a steady flow around the vessel in one smooth arc, starting at the base (now at the top) and moving down the outside. Rotate the piece slightly during the pour so the glaze covers the full circumference.
Lower the piece right-way-up onto a bat or board. Clean the foot ring immediately with a damp sponge if no wax resist was applied.
Check for thin patches: the glaze surface should look even and matte when wet. Touch up any thin spots with a single coat from the liner brush. Let the glaze dry fully before loading into the kiln.

items.problem: Glaze coat is uneven with thick drips on one side
items.cause: The pour speed was inconsistent or the vessel was not rotated during the pour
items.fix: Remove excess glaze by scraping gently at leather-hard glaze consistency with a fingernail, or blend thick drips by blotting lightly with a barely damp sponge. Next time, move the jug in a smooth arc and rotate the piece during the pour to spread the flow

items.problem: Piece sticks to the kiln shelf after firing
items.cause: Glaze was not cleaned from the foot ring
items.fix: Chip the piece off the shelf carefully. Grind the stuck glaze from the foot ring with a diamond pad. Keep foot rings clean before loading next time.
